rows.statement: Know that atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
rows.misconception: A good microscope can show an atom.

rows.statement: Know that the number of protons tells you which element an atom is.
rows.misconception: Elements are made of different kinds of stuff.

rows.statement: Know that changing the number of protons changes the element.
rows.misconception: An atom stays the same element when it gains or loses a proton.

rows.statement: Know that atoms of one element have the same protons but can have different neutrons, and that these are called isotopes.
rows.misconception: Atoms of one element are all identical.

rows.statement: Know that an isotope is not automatically radioactive: most of the atoms around us are stable isotopes.
rows.misconception: Isotope means radioactive or man-made.

rows.statement: Know that ordinary matter, including air, is made of atoms, and that light and heat are not.
rows.misconception: Air is nothing, so only solid things are made of atoms.

rows.statement: Know that the tiny nucleus at the centre holds almost all of an atom's mass, and that the rest of the atom is mostly empty space.
rows.misconception: An atom is a solid ball.

rows.statement: Name the three particles of an atom and say whether each is positive, negative or has no charge.
rows.misconception: Every atom is made of its own kind of stuff.

rows.statement: Know that some combinations of protons and neutrons make a stable nucleus and others make an unstable one.
rows.misconception: Every atom stays the same for ever.

rows.statement: Know that an unstable nucleus can change and give off radiation, and that this happens naturally.
rows.misconception: Radioactivity is something people create, and anything nuclear is dangerous.

rows.statement: Know that a daughter can be unstable and decay again, until a stable nucleus is reached (a decay chain).
rows.misconception: Every decay makes a stable atom.

rows.statement: Know that a decay changes a nucleus into a different one; nothing simply vanishes.
rows.misconception: Decay means the atom disappears.

rows.statement: Know that half-life describes a group, not a timer in each nucleus.
rows.misconception: A radioactive atom waits exactly one half-life before it decays.

rows.statement: Know that half-life is the time for about half of a large group of radioactive nuclei to decay.
rows.misconception: A radioactive atom is half gone after one half-life.

rows.statement: Read the pattern 100, 50, 25, 12 and know that radioactivity fades but is not gone after one half-life.
rows.misconception: After one half-life the radioactivity is gone, and radioactive material stays radioactive for ever.

rows.statement: Name natural places radioactivity and radiation come from: rocks and soil, radon in air, food and the body, space.
rows.misconception: Radioactivity is something humans created, and it only exists in nuclear facilities.

rows.statement: Know that radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous; it depends on the type, the amount and how it reaches the body.
rows.misconception: Radioactive means automatically dangerous.

rows.statement: Name the nucleus that decays (parent) and the nucleus it becomes (daughter).
Know that alpha and beta are particles and gamma is electromagnetic radiation, so the three are different.
rows.misconception: Alpha, beta and gamma are the same thing, and gamma is made of tiny pieces of the nucleus.

rows.statement: Know that you cannot predict when one particular nucleus will decay, although a large group follows a pattern.
rows.misconception: If you watch a nucleus closely you can tell when it will change.

rows.statement: Say what each one is: alpha is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, beta is a fast electron, gamma is high-energy electromagnetic radiation.
rows.misconception: The electron of a beta particle was orbiting the nucleus.

rows.statement: Know that an unstable nucleus changes by itself: nobody has to trigger it.
rows.misconception: Decay can be switched on and off, or a person has to make an atom decay.

rows.statement: Know that a radiation detector picks up some radiation almost anywhere, because background radiation is always present.
rows.misconception: A detector that picks up radiation must be right next to a dangerous source.

rows.statement: Know that radiation is detected and measured with instruments: a Geiger counter detects ionization in a gas, a scintillation counter detects flashes of light, and a dosimeter is worn to measure a person's exposure.
rows.misconception: We can see or feel ionizing radiation without an instrument.

rows.statement: Know that exposure to a source outside you ends when the source is shielded or you move away, and that a contaminated person is exposed until the radioactive material is removed.
rows.misconception: Exposure to radiation lasts after you leave the source.

rows.statement: Know that being exposed to radiation from a source is different from being contaminated, which means radioactive material is on or in something.
rows.misconception: Standing near a radioactive source makes you radioactive.

rows.statement: Know that gamma rays pass through thin barriers and need thick, dense material such as lead or concrete, and that the right shield depends on the kind of radiation.
rows.misconception: Anything solid is a good shield against all radiation.

rows.statement: Know that ionizing radiation has enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, and that weaker radiation does not.
rows.misconception: All radiation is the same.

rows.statement: Know that alpha particles are stopped by paper or skin, beta particles by a thin layer of metal, and that gamma rays are the most penetrating of the three.
rows.misconception: One kind of shield stops every kind of radiation.

rows.statement: Tell which common kinds of radiation are ionizing (alpha, beta, gamma and X-rays) and which are not (radio waves, microwaves and visible light).
rows.misconception: If something is called radiation, it must be dangerous.

rows.statement: Match the becquerel, the gray and the sievert to what each measures: how active a source is, how much energy is absorbed, and the potential for harm.
rows.misconception: The becquerel, the gray and the sievert all measure the same thing.

rows.statement: Know that a large number of becquerels does not by itself tell you how much energy a body absorbs or how much harm it could do, because those have their own units.
rows.misconception: A source with a large becquerel number is automatically harmful to anyone near it.

rows.statement: Know that ionizing radiation has enough energy to damage the molecules in a cell, including its DNA, and that being exposed to radiation does not make a person radioactive.
rows.misconception: Radiation that passes through a body leaves the person radioactive.

rows.statement: Know that cells are very good at repairing radiation damage, and that damage which is not repaired correctly can kill a cell or eventually make it cancerous.
rows.misconception: Radiation damage can never be repaired.

rows.statement: Know that doses come in very different sizes: a year near a nuclear power station is under 0.01 millisieverts, an average year about 6, a whole-body CT about 10, and about 1000 millisieverts (1 sievert) in a short time is where people start to become ill.
rows.misconception: A small dose and a dangerous dose are the same thing.

rows.statement: Know that everyone gets a small dose of radiation every day, mostly from natural sources, and that the average yearly dose in the US is about 6 millisieverts.
rows.misconception: Only people who work with radiation get a dose.

rows.statement: Know that a very large dose in a short time, about 1 sievert or more, makes people ill, with symptoms such as nausea and vomiting within hours, and that how fast a dose arrives (the dose rate) matters as well as how big it is.
rows.misconception: Only the total dose matters, not how fast it arrives.

rows.statement: Pick which of time, distance or shielding a real situation uses, such as a lead apron at a dental X-ray, sources stored under water or in concrete, or a shelter with more walls.
rows.misconception: Time, distance and shielding are only ideas for experts, not things used in everyday life.

rows.statement: Know that both 'any dose of radiation is deadly' and 'radiation is harmless' are wrong: the size and the speed of the dose decide what happens.
rows.misconception: Any dose of radiation is deadly.

rows.statement: Know that low doses do not cause immediate illness but can add a small chance of cancer over a lifetime, and that a dose that is low or spread over a long time carries less risk, because repair is more likely.
rows.misconception: A small dose every day is the same as one large dose.

rows.statement: Know three questions to ask about any dose in a headline: how big it is in millisieverts, how fast it arrived, and how it compares with doses you know.
rows.misconception: A scary headline about radiation tells you how big the dose is.

rows.statement: Know the three ways to lower a dose: spend less time near the source, stay farther from it, or put a shield between you and it.
rows.misconception: Nothing can be done to lower a dose.
